questions.prompt: Complete this suggestion: "___ join the school reading club?"
questions.explanation: "Why not" is right: this structure is followed by the base verb alone, with nothing in between — Why not join the school reading club? "Why not to" adds the to that the structure never takes, "Why not you" slips in a subject that a suggestion does not need, and "What about" must be followed by a noun or an -ing verb, so it cannot stand before the base form join.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Did you write your resolutions for the term? — ___"
questions.explanation: "Yes, I did." is right: a short answer repeats the helper of the question, and this question begins with Did. "Yes, I do." moves the helper to the present, "Yes, I am." borrows the verb be, which is not in the question at all, and "Yes, I wrote." repeats the main verb instead of the helper.

questions.prompt: Which sentence says that you understood a large part of the lesson, but not all of it?
questions.explanation: "I understood most of it." is right: most of it covers a large part of the lesson but still leaves something out. "I understood everything." leaves nothing out at all, "I understood only a little." sits at the other end of the scale, where you caught very little, and "I understood nothing at all." says you caught none of it.

questions.prompt: Complete this resolution: "From now on I ___ longer texts in English."
questions.explanation: "will read" is right: a resolution is will followed by the base verb, and nothing comes between the two — From now on I will read longer texts in English. "will to read" inserts a to, "will reads" adds the present -s that a base form never carries, and "will reading" puts an -ing form where the base form belongs.

questions.prompt: Your classmate says: "The second text was too long." What does she mean?

options.text: It was very long, and that was fine.
It was exactly the right length.
It was shorter than she needed.
It was longer than she wanted.

questions.explanation: "It was longer than she wanted." is right: too is not very — it means more than I want, so too long is a complaint and not a neutral fact. "It was very long, and that was fine." is what very long would say, "It was exactly the right length." is what the right length means, and "It was shorter than she needed." is the idea carried by too short.
